props.title: Claire's Camera
props.initialSlug: A chance encounter at the Cannes Film Festival

sections.content: **Claire's Camera (2017)** (2017) represents Hong Sang-soo's masterful exploration of chance encounters and subtle human connection, shot guerrilla-style during the Cannes Film Festival. Kim Min-hee delivers a nuanced performance as Manhee, a film sales agent abruptly fired from her job, whose path crosses with Isabelle Huppert's Claire, a French teacher with a Polaroid camera. The film echoes the spontaneous spirit of the French New Wave, particularly **Agnès Varda's** slice-of-life documentaries like **Faces Places** (2017) and the intimate character studies of **Eric Rohmer's** summer tales. On the Beach at Night Alone|2017|Another Hong Sang-soo and Kim Min-hee collaboration exploring personal crisis through chance meetings|MUBI Right Now, Wrong Then|2015|A director meets a painter, leading to two versions of the same day|Criterion The Day After|2017|A publishing house becomes entangled in romantic complications|MUBI

Hong's signature style of repeated encounters and shifting perspectives finds perfect expression in this compact 69-minute feature. Like his earlier work **The Day He Arrives** (2011), the film uses seemingly casual interactions to reveal deeper truths about human relationships. The Polaroid camera becomes both a plot device and metaphor for capturing fleeting moments, similar to how Abbas Kiarostami used photography in **24 Frames** (2017) to explore time and perception. SUBHEAD: The Power of Simple Observation

Claire's role as an observer with her camera mirrors Hong's own filmmaking approach - deceptively simple yet profound. This technique recalls the observational style of **Yasujirō Ozu's** late films like **An Autumn Afternoon** (1962), where small moments carry immense emotional weight. The beachside setting of Cannes becomes another character, much like how Hong used locations in **In Another Country** (2012) to explore cultural disconnection and serendipitous meetings.
